comment.name: Millard J Melnyk
comment.body:
I'm tired to death of this idea of "support". 

The fact that you have an opinion that agrees or disagrees with an idea, a movement, a group of people, a situation etc., means exactly diddly squat. 

The idea that it's important and makes a difference to anything material is all kinds of narcissistic. 

No, you don't matter that much, and I don't matter that much. 

The fact that you or I have an opinion has no bearing on the questions: 

1. Should we have an opinion? 

2. Are we qualified to have an opinion? 

3. Does our opinion reflect reality or contradict it?

4. Is it smart?

5. Is it crazy? 

6. Should other people have the same opinion? 

7. If everyone had the same opinion, would that be a good thing or a fiasco? 

I could go on and on with questions that everybody seems to take for granted in the mere fact that they present an opinion or "take a stand" or express support.

As if the fact that they did so is about the most important thing a person could do. 

Well, I'm here to say that if that's the most important thing you can think of doing, you've done exactly fuckall -- the irony being that you think you've done everything. 

And the proof that you think you did everything lies in the fact that you do absofuckinglootely nothing more.

comment.name: Millard J Melnyk
comment.body:
Most people, I would think, consider statements like these as proof that our current systems have severely malfunctioned.

I don't, because that would imply they were intended to do other than they do.

If they were otherwise intended, they would have been fixed already -- or else those responsible for them are bloody incompetent, idiotic, and useless.

So, you get your choice: either the systems and their creators and operators -- your "leaders" -- are evil, or they're completely out of control, being bumbling fucking morons. 

Lunatics, actually, because only lunatics could want and intend the kind of harm these systems do with oodles of support and cooperation but practically zero resistance.

Either way, why do you insist on "following" such "leaders" and defending them?

I have never once heard a convincing, cogent, competent answer to that question. All answers ended up boiling down to codependence. 

But that entire discussion is completely beside the point that really matters.

What matters is our psychosis. 

The way we think about our systems is not just irrational. Irrationality implies randomness, lack of control and sense, so therefore, lack of consistent, reliable direction. No, this is perverse irrationality: consistently precise opposition to what's beneficial, functional, and sane.

The proof? 

In every case of horrific evildoing, by the time our systems, whether they're moral or religious or legal or social, come around to finally admitting what's been happening -- long before anyone has even begun to deal with it, having only just admitted it -- the evil's been done.

No one is protected, no evils are prevented, no victims are saved -- nothing.

This isn't an accident or an unfortunate limitation or an unavoidable inevitability. 

This is the design. We create systems that guarantee that EVERYONE will get away with it for at least a while. And then we apply a completely self-serving, nonsensical, and useless practice called "punishment", as if it makes things better when all it does is increase net detriment.

We're convinced this is the best we can do and better than doing nothing at all -- but that's not our psychosis.

Our psychosis is that we refuse to investigate completely different kinds of systems, being certain before any investigation that there's no point in investigating them, and never once wonder how we became so certain or whether the sources of our certainty are wise or crazy.

comment.name: Millard J Melnyk
comment.body:
Most of us begin by countering violence on the same level as the aggression. This is where we start, but we need to make sure it's not where we end.

In this mindfucked world, "power" means violence used to dominate. The goal of "power" is always to dominate and, if possible, to achieve complete control.

This is something that only psychotics are drawn to, and something that seems sensible only to them.

We need to get to the point where we're not threatened by violence anymore and become fully confident that we can deal with it. We make that progress by dealing with aggression on the level it's dealt out. But this is the level of opposing, not not the level of overcoming.

To overcome violence, you need to drop down a level and attack the assumptions on which the aggression was predicated.

This does 3 things.

First, it immediately deflates the aggression, because it's looking for retaliation on that same level where it was dealt out. When we respond on a more fundamental level, the aggressor has nothing to fight at that level, now -- the only level that makes sense to them.

So, second, it baffles and demoralizes the aggressor because they literally do not know what the fuck is going on.

Third, it draws the focus of the confrontation down towards the actual reasons for the aggression, which are always buried beneath the aggressor's psychosis that created it, below the level where the psychosis expresses in behavior. Now the question isn't about the status (right/wrong, true/false, good/evil) of the aggressive actions, but the assumptions, intentions, and motivations that gave rise to the actions.

Of course, a person who reads this will likely want an example of how to do this with someone that's about to punch them in the nose, which is curious -- because, when was the last time someone was about to punch them in the nose? 😆

I think the last time I faced a meathead that wanted to do me bodily harm was back in the early 00s when a guy that came at me with a golf club while I was sitting in my car.
